::: {#rem-theory-of-computation}
#### Where state machines come from

The theory of computation [@wikipedia_theory_of_computation] asks what computers can do.
It has three parts:

- *computability theory* asks which problems a computer can solve at all.
  For example, no program can decide, for every program $P$ and input $I$, whether $P$ stops when it runs on $I$;
  this is the halting problem [@wikipedia_halting_problem].
- *complexity theory* asks how much time the problems that can be solved need.
  Whether every problem whose answers can be checked quickly can also be solved quickly
  is the P versus NP problem [@wikipedia_p_versus_np_problem], which no one had solved as of 2026.
- *automata theory* makes "computer" and "problem" precise, so that the other two parts can prove things about them.
  A computer becomes an abstract machine, called an *automaton* (plural *automata*),
  and a problem becomes the question of which strings (@def-string) the machine answers yes for.

The halting problem and the P versus NP problem are about machines that can do anything a general program can,
called Turing machines [@wikipedia_turing_machine].
This chapter studies the simplest automata, which remember only one of finitely many situations.
They are far less powerful than Turing machines, and cannot model a general program.

:::
